common_name: Miss Manners Obedient Plant (Clumping Non-Spreading False Dragonhead)

planting.note: Plant divisions or nursery starts in spring or early fall in moist, humus-rich soil; unlike the wild species and most cultivars, this selection stays in a tight clump instead of spreading by rhizomes.

directions: Set out divisions in average to moist garden soil and water regularly during the first season to establish; established clumps tolerate both moist low spots and normal border conditions. Pinch stems in late spring to encourage bushier, sturdier growth and more flower spikes. Pure white, hinged, snapdragon-like flowers open from the bottom of the spike upward from mid to late summer and are a favorite of bumblebees. This cultivar is prized specifically because it lacks the aggressive rhizomatous spread that makes the straight species and older cultivars a garden thug, making it far better suited to mixed perennial borders.

common_name: Venusta Queen of the Prairie (Deep Pink Meadowsweet Cultivar)

planting.note: Plant divisions in spring into consistently moist, rich soil; this cultivar wants more water than most perennials and thrives at pond edges, in rain gardens, or low wet meadow spots.

directions: Give this selection steady moisture and rich soil; it struggles and scorches in dry conditions but forms an impressive stand of coarse, astilbe-like foliage topped by feathery deep-pink plumes in early to midsummer where sited well. Divide congested clumps every few years in spring or fall to maintain vigor and control spread. It is an excellent architectural plant for the back of a moist border or a rain garden, and its plumes are noticeably deeper pink than the species. Bees and butterflies visit the frothy flower heads, and the seed heads provide additional late-season texture.

planting.note: Set out nursery divisions in spring after frost danger has passed; this compact selection tolerates both average garden soil and periodic wet feet, unlike many border perennials.

directions: This University of Arkansas introduction forms a tidy, rounded mound of fine, threadlike foliage that looks almost like a dwarf conifer until it is topped with masses of small purple button flowers in late summer. Plant in full sun in well-drained to occasionally moist soil; it is far more compact and floriferous than the straight species and needs no staking. It is an outstanding late-season nectar source for butterflies, including migrating monarchs, and its fine texture makes it a good foil for bolder-leaved prairie companions. Cut back in late winter before new growth emerges.
sources: University of Arkansas Division of Agriculture

common_name: Tropic Sun Sunn Hemp (Low-Alkaloid Non-Naturalizing Sunn Hemp)

planting.note: Broadcast or drill after soil has warmed well past last frost; this cultivar was bred specifically to flower later and set less viable seed than common sunn hemp, reducing volunteer/weed risk.

directions: Drill or broadcast seed at a dense rate into warm soil for rapid, weed-suppressing canopy closure; this fast-growing tropical legume can add substantial biomass and fix significant nitrogen within 60-90 days. Tropic Sun was developed by the USDA-NRCS Hawaii Plant Materials Center and University of Hawaii specifically as a low-alkaloid, later-flowering selection that is far less prone to naturalizing than wild-type sunn hemp, making it the standard cultivar recommended for mainland US cover cropping. Mow or crimp before or at early flowering to prevent seed set and to maximize the tender, quickly decomposing biomass; it is killed by frost. It is especially valued for suppressing root-knot nematodes and breaking up compacted soil with its vigorous taproot.

common_name: Marshall Annual Ryegrass (Georgia-Bred Cold-Tolerant Italian Ryegrass)

planting.note: Drill or broadcast in early fall for winter cover, or in early spring where summers stay cool; this cultivar is more winter-hardy and later-maturing than common annual ryegrass.

directions: Broadcast or drill into a prepared or no-till seedbed in early fall for a dense, fibrous-rooted winter cover that scavenges leftover nitrogen and improves soil tilth. Marshall is an older, widely grown Georgia-developed selection valued for better winter survival and later spring maturity than common annual ryegrass, giving a longer window of grazing or biomass production before it heads out. Terminate by mowing, herbicide, or crimping before seed set in spring to avoid it becoming a weedy volunteer in the following crop. Its extensive fibrous root system is particularly effective at reducing soil compaction and erosion on row-crop ground over winter.
sources: Oregon State University Seed Certification Service

common_name: Kopu II White Clover (Large-Leaved Grazing and Cover Crop White Clover)

planting.note: Broadcast into a firm, weed-free seedbed in early spring or late summer; shallow seeding depth is essential since seed is very small and this large-leaved type establishes more slowly than small-leaved white clovers.

directions: Broadcast or drill shallowly into a well-prepared seedbed; this New Zealand-bred large-leaved white clover establishes a persistent, high-yielding stand valued in pastures and living mulches alike. Its bigger leaves and stolons give it greater drought tolerance and yield than common Dutch white clover while still fixing substantial nitrogen and tolerating grazing or mowing. Interseed with grasses or use as a standalone living mulch between rows in orchards and vegetable beds; it spreads by surface stolons and persists for multiple seasons where winters are not extreme. Mow periodically to prevent grasses or weeds from shading it out and to encourage continued stolon spread.
